1-1: ISO 8373 defines a robot as a programmed actuated mechanism with a degree of autonomy to perform locomotion, manipulation or positioning.
Autonomy measures a machine's ability to perform intended tasks based on current state and sensing without human intervention.
Robots operate through a sense, think, act loop where sensors measure conditions, controllers make decisions, and actuators execute motion.
Control architectures organize robot decision-making into sense-plan-act, reactive subsumption, or hybrid three-layer systems.
1-2: Early automata and Jacquard's punched cards introduced stored programs that let machines change behavior without being rebuilt.
Unimate became the first industrial robot in 1961, handling hot die-cast parts at General Motors.
The robotics industry shifted during the 1970s from hydraulic actuators to electrically powered, computer-controlled robot arms.
Universal Robots introduced the UR5 in 2008 as the first commercially viable collaborative robot that worked without safety cages.
Mobile robotics progressed from early research robots like Shakey to commercial warehouse systems and planetary rovers.
1-3: Industrial robots are classified primarily by mechanical structure into articulated, SCARA, Cartesian, parallel delta, cylindrical, and polar types.
Robot spec sheets define mechanical capability through key metrics including payload, reach, repeatability, and cycle time.
Safety standards define collaborative applications rather than collaborative robots, requiring risk assessments for the entire work task.
Automated Guided Vehicles follow fixed physical guides, whereas Autonomous Mobile Robots map environments and dynamically plan paths around obstacles.
1-4: Python and C++ serve as the primary programming languages for ROS 2 nodes and microcontroller code.
Robot kinematics relies on trigonometry, vectors, matrices, and calculus to calculate positions, orientations, and velocities.
Simulators such as URSim and Gazebo let engineers test code safely before deploying to physical robots.
Industrial robots communicate with controllers and peripherals over standard network protocols such as Modbus TCP and EtherNet/IP.
1-5: Global industrial robot installations reached 603,307 in 2025, bringing the operational stock past five million robots.
Robot density measures operational industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees, with the Republic of Korea leading at 1,220 in 2024.
Handling represents the largest industrial robot application, while electrical and automotive manufacturing buy the most robots.
Medical systems such as da Vinci operate via teleoperation where human surgeons directly control instruments from a console.
Extreme environments rely on specialized robots for deep space exploration, disaster response, and hazardous nuclear site investigations.
1-6: A rigid object in three-dimensional space has six degrees of freedom, requiring six robot axes to control position and orientation.
Pose accuracy measures distance from a commanded target, whereas pose repeatability measures how closely repeated visits cluster together.
Setting up tool frames at the tool center point and work objects on fixtures makes robot motion programs reusable.
Forward kinematics calculates tool pose from joint angles, whereas inverse kinematics calculates required joint angles for a desired pose.
Motion instructions interpolate paths via joint, linear, or circular moves, using zone blending to smooth transitions without stopping.
1-7: An industrial robot cell combines a robot manipulator with end-of-arm tooling, part presentation, controllers, and safeguarding to perform specific tasks.
A cell programmable logic controller coordinates operations with the robot through handshake signals while safety interlocks communicate along a separate dedicated path.
Commissioning a turnkey cell includes a factory acceptance test at the integrator facility and a site acceptance test at the customer plant.
Cell cycle time depends on the slowest bottleneck operation, which must remain at or below customer takt time.
Tooling, controls, safeguarding, programming, and system integration typically represent the majority of a robot cell's total cost.
2-1: Online programming teaches target points directly on the physical robot using a teach pendant or manual lead-through.
Offline programming generates and simulates robot programs within 3D CAD environments without interrupting active production.
Bridging the simulation-to-reality gap requires calibration of tool center points, work objects, and robot kinematics.
Post-processors translate simulated paths from offline software into brand-specific languages like RAPID or URScript.
Block-based visual tools enable operators to build robot programs quickly using drag-and-drop programming nodes.
2-2: ABB RobotStudio uses a Virtual Controller running the actual RobotWare software to simulate motions and calculate cycle times accurately.
Universal Robots PolyScope structures robot programs as visual trees where operators teach waypoints using Freedrive hand guiding.
Virtual commissioning connects simulation models to programmable logic controllers to validate cell interlocks and communication before physical installation.
The URCaps ecosystem lets third-party developers add custom hardware plugins and interface nodes directly into PolyScope.
Brand-agnostic platforms like RoboDK generate vendor-specific robot code across multiple manufacturers through specialized post-processors.
2-3: Industrial robot makers develop proprietary languages to execute motion logic reliably within strict real-time controller cycles.
ABB RAPID structures programs into tasks, modules, and routines while using robtarget types to specify Cartesian poses and configurations.
Universal Robots URScript uses Python-like syntax and rotation vectors to define spatial orientations in standard metric units.
KUKA Robot Language separates program logic in source files from permanent coordinate targets stored in matching data files.
FANUC pairs simple Teach Pendant motion programs on the shop floor with compiled KAREL programs for complex communication.
2-4: ROS provides open-source robot middleware that abstracts hardware interfaces and promotes algorithm reuse across different robot brands.
ROS 2 replaces the centralized roscore master with Data Distribution Service to enable distributed discovery and configurable Quality of Service.
The four pillars of ROS encompass plumbing middleware, developer tools, reusable algorithm capabilities, and a global open-source ecosystem.
Community stacks like Nav2 for mobile robots and MoveIt 2 for arms solve complex navigation and manipulation problems.
ROS-Industrial provides production-grade open-source drivers and interfaces to bridge standard industrial manipulators with advanced ROS 2 capabilities.
2-5: Gripper families include vacuum cups, mechanical finger grippers, magnetic tools, and soft compliant grippers tailored to specific workpieces.
Vacuum gripper sizing calculates required holding force from workpiece mass, robot acceleration, and friction safety factors.
Standardized tool flanges conforming to ISO 9409-1 provide mechanical mounting patterns for robotic end-of-arm tooling.
Robot controllers require accurate tool center point, payload mass, and center of gravity configurations to maintain dynamic path accuracy.
Reliable pick programs never move away until digital input sensors confirm successful part gripping within a defined timeout.
2-6: A standard pick-and-place cycle combines fast joint approach moves, slow linear descents, exact stops, and vertical retractions.
Robot simulators like URSim in Docker and ABB RobotStudio execute real controller code without requiring physical hardware.
Programmers must always execute exact stops without blending at positions where grippers actuate or release workpieces.
Computing approach points with offsets such as RelTool or pose_trans keeps them tied to the taught grip position.
Teaching target points relative to a three-point fixture frame allows moving the fixture without re-teaching individual waypoints.
2-7: ABB RAPID organizes robot logic into modular files containing procedures, functions, trap interrupt handlers, and typed declarations.
RAPID storage types determine persistence: CONST remains unchangeable, VAR resets upon returning to main, and PERS survives restarts.
Palletizing routines compute matrix slot positions from a single taught corner using integer division and modulo math with coordinate offsets.
Structured error handling in RAPID uses ERROR blocks and ERRNO codes to manage failures via RETRY, TRYNEXT, RETURN, or RAISE.
Production programs prevent infinite retry loops by limiting attempts, notifying operators with messages, and stopping safely.
2-8: Vision-guided robotics locates parts with cameras and shifts robot frames dynamically without altering underlying motion paths.
System designers select between fixed eye-to-hand cameras and wrist-mounted eye-in-hand cameras based on cycle time and field of view.
Intrinsic camera calibration determines the camera matrix and models lens distortion to map raw image pixels accurately.
Hand-eye calibration solves the AX = XB equation to link camera coordinates with the robot manipulator coordinate system.
Adjusting pick positions requires full rigid transformations with translations and rotations rather than adding simple Cartesian offsets.
3-1: A software repository requires an open source license to grant legal permissions to inspect, modify, and share code.
Public open-source contributions provide visible evidence of technical ability and collaborative communication skills.
Standard repository files include LICENSE for permissions, README.md for project overview, CONTRIBUTING for development processes, and CODE_OF_CONDUCT for community behavior.
ROS 2 packages standardly adopt permissive software licenses such as the Apache 2.0 license to maximize reuse.
3-2: Non-code contributions like documentation improvements, issue triaging, and peer reviews offer accessible ways to support open-source robotics projects.
Issue labels such as first-timers-only, good first issue, and help wanted guide newcomers toward manageable initial tasks.
The GitHub contribution workflow involves forking the repository, cloning locally, connecting the upstream remote, and creating an edit branch.
Opening draft pull requests early invites constructive reviewer feedback while frequent upstream pulls prevent merge conflicts.
Open-source etiquette requires keeping technical discussions public, providing reproduction steps, and commenting on issues before starting work.
3-3: ROS 2 packages maintain distribution-specific release branches where breaking API changes are prohibited to guarantee software stability.
New features and bug fixes land first in the rolling development branch before developers backport them to stable releases.
Quality standards defined in REP 2004 govern testing requirements verified continuously on the automated ROS 2 build farm.
Submitting contributions requires a Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off, peer review approval, and clean Git commit history without force-pushing.
3-4: Beginners can make first open-source contributions by fixing typos, suggesting verified sources, or reporting broken links.
Contributors can submit small documentation fixes directly in web browsers using the GitHub Propose changes interface without local setup.
Working locally with Git allows contributors to test changes and run verification scripts before pushing commits upstream.
Every factual claim added to robOSStics must trace to an entry in docs/sources.json to maintain site accuracy.
Contributors should never hand-edit generated regions like sitemap.xml, instead letting scripts update those files automatically.
3-5: Nav2 provides the flagship autonomous mobile robot navigation framework in ROS 2, maintained by Open Navigation LLC.
Mobile robot navigation combines state estimation coordinate transforms, 2D costmaps, path planners, trajectory controllers, and recovery behaviors.
Behavior trees organize navigation execution through hierarchical logic to verify and validate complex robot decision sequences.
Nav2 packages use plugin interfaces for custom algorithms, with code licensed under Apache-2.0 or BSD-3-Clause and requiring DCO sign-offs.
Contributing to Nav2 follows a structured path of opening an issue, claiming the task, and submitting pull requests.
4-1: ROS functions as robot middleware that coordinates independent modular processes called nodes across host operating systems.
Nodes exchange continuous data streams anonymously using strongly typed messages over named publish-subscribe topics.
Services execute synchronous or asynchronous request-response transactions suitable for short one-off operations.
Actions manage long-running tasks by providing continuous feedback along with the ability to cancel or preempt goals.
The ROS_DOMAIN_ID environment variable isolates network traffic across distinct robot systems sharing the same local network subnet.
4-2: ROS 2 replaces centralized roscore discovery with peer-to-peer Data Distribution Service middleware to eliminate single points of failure.
The ROS Middleware abstraction layer allows developers to select different communication implementations via the RMW_IMPLEMENTATION environment variable.
Configurable Quality of Service policies govern message delivery reliability, durability, and queue depth for each individual communication endpoint.
Communication requires compatible Quality of Service profiles where publishers must offer equal or higher guarantees than subscribers request.
Managed lifecycle nodes transition through Unconfigured, Inactive, Active, and Finalized states under supervisor control for safe system startup.
4-3: ROS 2 categorizes host platforms into three support tiers, targeting Ubuntu Linux as the primary Tier 1 operating system.
Desktop installations provide visualization tools like RViz alongside communication libraries, whereas base installations omit graphical utilities for headless computers.
Sourcing the setup.bash file configures essential shell environment variables including PATH, PYTHONPATH, and AMENT_PREFIX_PATH to locate ROS commands.
Workspace development requires colcon to build multi-package projects and rosdep to resolve external system dependencies defined in package manifests.
Troubleshooting communication failures between nodes entails checking environment variables, matching domain identifiers, and verifying local network multicast permissions.
4-4: Turtlesim provides a lightweight two-dimensional simulation environment for practicing node communication without risking physical hardware.
Keyboard teleoperation publishes velocity commands as Twist messages containing linear and angular vectors to control robot motion.
Command-line remapping redirects topic and service names at startup, enabling software reuse across different robots without modifying source code.
A standard ROS 2 workspace organizes user packages in a source folder alongside build, install, and log directories.
Custom Python nodes inherit from rclpy Node classes to manage publishers, subscribers, and periodic timers.
4-5: RViz2 renders live sensor readings, occupancy maps, and robot models in three dimensions relative to a stationary Fixed Frame.
The tf2 library tracks spatial relationships between coordinate frames over time to let tools transform sensor data across links.
The rqt_graph plugin diagrams active node connections and communication topics to reveal graph topology and disconnected interfaces.
The ros2 bag utility records message traffic into MCAP storage files for deterministic telemetry replay and offline algorithm testing.
Gazebo simulates environmental physics and virtual sensors, exchanging data with ROS 2 through the ros_gz bridge interface.
4-6: ROS 2 workspaces layer user packages as an overlay that overrides matching packages in the underlying core installation.
Running ros2 pkg create with the ament_python build type generates the manifest, setup scripts, and module directory for Python nodes.
Declaring runtime dependencies in package.xml enables rosdep to discover and install required system libraries before building.
Using rclpy.init as a context manager starts the ROS client library and shuts it down cleanly when the node ends.
Open-loop state machine controllers accumulate position drift over time, requiring sensor feedback to achieve accurate path tracking.
4-7: ROS 2 launch files coordinate starting and monitoring multiple nodes across distributed processes through Python, XML, or YAML descriptions.
Python launch files implement a generate_launch_description function that returns a LaunchDescription containing Node actions, namespaces, and remappings.
Substitutions and launch arguments evaluate dynamically at runtime, allowing operators to modify node behavior directly from the command line.
Individual nodes declare and manage their own parameters locally instead of storing configurations on a centralized global parameter server.
Parameter files use YAML formatting with fully qualified node names and ros__parameters keys to load startup configurations.
4-8: MoveIt 2 calculates collision-free trajectories and joint angles to move robotic manipulators toward specified goals.
The URDF defines mechanical geometry and limits, whereas the SRDF specifies semantic planning groups and disabled collision pairs.
The ros2_control framework bridges trajectory controllers with physical actuators or software mock hardware interfaces.
The move_group node integrates planning scene models, inverse kinematics solvers, and trajectory generation adapters.
Planners include randomized OMPL algorithms for obstacle avoidance and deterministic Pilz generators for linear or point-to-point Cartesian motions.
4-9: ROS-Industrial provides open-source packages and tools to integrate commercial industrial manipulators into the ROS 2 software ecosystem.
Vendor drivers share a three-layer architecture combining controller programs, ros2_control hardware interfaces, and standardized trajectory controllers.
The FollowJointTrajectory action interface serves as the standard abstraction for passing timed joint-space trajectories to robot controllers.
Streaming drivers require low-latency Linux kernels to meet cyclic control deadlines and prevent communication timeouts with the controller.
Industrial applications often combine vendor languages for cell sequence logic with ROS 2 planners for perception-driven motion segments.
5-1: The NSPE and IEEE codes of ethics mandate that engineers hold paramount public safety, health, and welfare above all commercial pressures.
Engineers must disclose all potential conflicts of interest promptly and practice strictly within their verified domains of technical competence.
The European Union Machinery Regulation establishes binding safety mandates addressing autonomous mobile machinery, cybersecurity risks, and self-evolving machine learning behaviors.
Strict product liability holds robotics manufacturers and system integrators legally accountable for injuries caused by design defects or insufficient warnings.
5-2: Layered functional safety architectures isolate non-safe application software from certified safety controllers and physical emergency stops.
Hardware watchdog timers trigger automated safe stops whenever main application control loops crash or become unresponsive.
Robotics perception pipelines must apply data minimization and on-device edge processing to protect bystander privacy.
Computer vision models require rigorous auditing across diverse demographic groups to mitigate algorithmic detection disparities in pedestrian detection.
The European Union AI Act classifies artificial intelligence safety components in industrial machinery as high-risk applications requiring strict human oversight.
5-3: Labor economists found adding one robot per thousand workers reduced the employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42%.
The task framework analyzes automation through competing displacement, productivity, and reinstatement mechanisms across production activities.
The reinstatement effect creates new complex occupations in which human workers maintain a comparative advantage over automated systems.
Data minimization and on-device edge computing reduce how much sensitive camera and map data a robot collects and sends.
The moral crumple zone concept describes how legal and moral blame disproportionately falls on human operators supervising autonomous machines.
5-5: Industrial artificial intelligence operates around the robot for perception, predictive maintenance, and programming assistance while safety controllers remain deterministic.
Vision-language-action foundation models translate multimodal prompts into actions but remain research platforms exhibiting run-to-run behavioral variance.
Large language models frequently hallucinate nonexistent functions and output subtle unit or coordinate frame errors in generated robot code.
Syntactically valid robot scripts can cause physical collisions if programmers fail to catch confused coordinate frames or swapped transform functions.
Engineers maintain full legal and ethical accountability for thoroughly verifying generated robot programs and recording their provenance.
6-1: Microcontrollers provide the predictable timing needed for low-level motor switching and fast sensor reading.
Microcontroller pins cannot drive motors directly because motors require high currents and produce damaging inductive spikes.
An H-bridge motor driver uses low-current signals from a microcontroller to switch high current from an external battery.
Connecting the Arduino ground and motor battery ground gives the driver a shared zero-volt reference for control signals.
Non-blocking timing using millis lets a robot read sensors continuously instead of freezing execution with delay.
6-2: Pulse Width Modulation rapidly switches between zero volts and full supply voltage to simulate intermediate analog voltages.
The duty cycle represents the percentage of each period the signal stays high, determining the average delivered voltage.
Microcontrollers rely on dedicated hardware timers to generate PWM waveforms without tying up the main processor in loops.
DC motors use PWM duty cycle to regulate speed, while RC servos use absolute pulse width at 50 Hz to command shaft position.
Using the Arduino Servo library on an Uno takes over Timer1 and disables analogWrite on pins 9 and 10.
6-3: Incremental encoders report relative movement and lose their position during power loss, requiring the robot to home.
Absolute encoders report an exact shaft position immediately on power-up without requiring homing moves.
Quadrature encoders generate two square waves offset by 90 degrees, allowing a controller to detect the direction of rotation.
Full quadrature decoding counts every rising and falling edge across both channels, producing four counts per pulse.
Hardware interrupts allow microcontrollers to count fast encoder pulses without dropping edges during main loop execution.
6-4: A PID controller combines present error, past accumulated error, and error rate of change to compute corrective actuator commands.
Pure proportional control leaves steady-state error, which the integral term eliminates by accumulating residual errors over time.
The derivative term opposes rapid error changes to damp oscillations, though it amplifies high-frequency sensor noise.
Anti-windup clamping prevents the integral term from accumulating excessive error while actuators operate at physical saturation limits.
Computing the derivative on the process measurement instead of error eliminates derivative kick when setpoints change abruptly.
6-5: Proprioceptive sensors measure internal robot states, while exteroceptive sensors detect physical properties of the external world.
Active sensors emit energy to measure returns in darkness, while passive sensors detect ambient environmental signals.
The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measures distance across a 15-degree cone, but smooth angled surfaces cause specular reflection.
Laser Time-of-Flight sensors measure photon transit times, making distance readings largely independent of target color and reflectance.
Integrating small zero-rate gyroscope biases over time causes heading drift that grows linearly unless corrected by sensor fusion.
6-6: Odometry calculates a mobile robot's pose by continuously adding up wheel motions measured by encoders.
In differential drive, average wheel travel gives center displacement, while the difference divided by wheelbase gives heading change.
Midpoint Runge-Kutta integration computes motion using the average heading halfway through the step to improve accuracy on curves.
Heading errors rotate future coordinate updates, making sideways position drift grow proportionally to the total distance traveled.
Systematic odometry errors come from physical robot dimensions and can be calibrated, whereas unpredictable wheel slip requires sensor fusion.
6-7: Finite state machines organize robot logic into distinct states, events, and guarded transitions so the robot occupies one state at a time.
Non-blocking timing using millis keeps the main loop running so controllers poll inputs and update timers without freezing execution.
Centralizing state transitions guarantees that entry timestamps and actuator commands are updated consistently.
ROS 2 managed nodes use four primary states—Unconfigured, Inactive, Active, and Finalized—to coordinate system bringup and shutdown.
Behavior trees route ticks through Sequence and Fallback control nodes to provide modular task execution and error recovery.
6-8: The Kalman filter combines a motion model prediction with noisy sensor measurements to produce an estimate more certain than either source alone.
The predict step projects the state forward while adding process noise, increasing estimation uncertainty.
The update step compares the sensor reading to the prediction and shrinks uncertainty using the Kalman gain.
The Kalman gain shifts trust toward the sensor when measurement noise is small, and toward the motion model when noise is large.
Non-linear robotic motion models use the Extended Kalman Filter through Jacobian linearization or the Unscented Kalman Filter using sigma points.
6-9: Motion profiles generate intermediate setpoints over time, separating the geometric path from how fast the robot moves along it.
A trapezoidal velocity profile accelerates, cruises, and decelerates, but short moves collapse into a triangular profile without a cruise phase.
S-curve profiles limit jerk by ramping acceleration gradually, reducing mechanical vibration and gearbox wear.
Joint moves follow straight lines in joint space, while linear moves guide the tool center point along Cartesian paths.
Blending zones allow a robot to round waypoints smoothly by overlapping deceleration of one move with acceleration of the next.
6-10: Forward kinematics calculates the tool position by summing rotating link vectors along the serial chain.
The reachable workspace of a planar two-link arm forms a ring bounded by the difference and sum of its link lengths.
Closed-form inverse kinematics uses the law of cosines and atan2 to find the elbow and shoulder angles.
Clamping the value passed to acos stops tiny rounding errors from crashing inverse kinematics code.
The Jacobian determinant equals zero when the arm is fully stretched or folded, marking singularities where radial movement is lost.
7-1: CMOS sensors offer fast pixel readout without blooming, while CCD sensors provide high pixel-to-pixel uniformity.
Global shutters expose every pixel simultaneously to eliminate motion distortion when imaging moving parts.
Increasing the lens f-number by the square root of two halves light throughput while expanding depth of field.
Telecentric lenses eliminate parallax and keep magnification constant even as part distance varies.
The GenICam standard provides a universal programming interface to control industrial cameras regardless of hardware manufacturer.
7-2: Proper illumination geometry improves vision system performance more effectively and economically than upgrading camera sensors or lenses.
Backlighting produces a high-contrast silhouette for measuring outer dimensions, but eliminates internal surface features.
Diffuse dome lights project omnidirectional light to eliminate glare and harsh shadows on curved, reflective parts.
Coaxial lighting uses a beamsplitter to project light along the camera axis, reducing glare on flat reflective objects.
Pulsed strobe operation lets lights overdrive LEDs up to 500 percent of nominal current to freeze motion while extending lifetime.
7-3: The HSV color space isolates chromatic hue from lighting intensity, enabling reliable color segmentation using inRange binary masks.
Otsu thresholding automatically calculates an optimal binarization cutoff on bimodal histograms, while adaptive thresholding adjusts for uneven scene lighting.
Image moments computed from extracted contours yield precise centroid coordinates for guiding robotic pick-and-place motions.
The Canny edge detector combines Gaussian smoothing, gradient calculations, non-maximum suppression, and hysteresis thresholding to produce clean single-pixel boundaries.
Template matching slides a reference patch across an image to locate parts based on visual correlation scores.
7-4: Direct 3D sensing determines depth from calibrated geometric baselines rather than unanchored neural network guesses.
Stereo vision calculates depth inversely proportional to horizontal disparity using baseline distance and focal length.
VoxelGrid filtering downsamples large point clouds into regular volumetric cubes to accelerate spatial processing.
RANSAC plane segmentation identifies and removes flat supporting surfaces like tables to isolate resting workpieces.
Euclidean cluster extraction groups segmented 3D points into individual objects based on spatial proximity.
7-5: Automated inspection reduces human visual inspection errors, which include missed defects and false alarms that cause production waste.
The Nyquist sampling limit requires at least two sensor pixels per optical line pair to resolve fine features without aliasing.
Telecentric lenses eliminate parallax error in precision gauging because their constant magnification prevents part height variations from altering measured dimensions.
Optical distortion displaces image features geometrically without blurring, allowing software calibration to rectify measurements.
Data Matrix ECC 200 uses Reed-Solomon error correction to read damaged symbols on direct part markings.
7-6: The ROS optical camera coordinate frame convention defines positive x pointing right, positive y pointing down, and positive z pointing forward.
CameraInfo messages supply intrinsic calibration matrices and plumb_bob distortion parameters to enable 3D geometric reconstruction.
The message_filters TimeSynchronizer matches image frames with calibration metadata by pairing messages that share identical header timestamps.
The cv_bridge package converts ROS Image messages to and from OpenCV NumPy arrays using imgmsg_to_cv2 and cv2_to_imgmsg.
Publishing processed images back to ROS requires preserving the original header timestamp and optical frame identifier.
8-1: In direct current circuits, sinking provides a path to supply common, whereas sourcing provides a path to positive supply.
NPN sinking field sensors require sourcing PLC inputs, while PNP sourcing sensors connect to sinking inputs.
Fieldbus networks replace bulky point-to-point wiring bundles by connecting multiple sensors and actuators across a single shared digital cable.
Cyclic communication exchanges real-time I/O data at fixed intervals, while acyclic communication transfers diagnostics and parameters on demand.
Device Level Ring networks use supervisor beacon frames to achieve fault recovery within 2890 µs across rings of up to 50 nodes.
8-2: EtherNet/IP separates time-critical implicit I/O data over UDP from acyclic explicit configuration requests over TCP.
PROFINET RT bypasses TCP/IP layers for millisecond determinism, while PROFINET IRT uses hardware switching for sub-millisecond motion control.
EtherCAT slave devices read and insert data on the fly as a single frame passes through the network.
Modbus TCP transmits big-endian registers and coils over TCP port 502 with a seven-byte MBAP header.
Engineering software imports standardized XML device description files like GSDML or ESI to configure field devices.
8-3: Universal Robots controllers connect to cell PLCs using EtherNet/IP implicit messaging, PROFINET modules, or Modbus TCP on port 502.
Up to 16 binary handshake signals can be packed into a single 16-bit Modbus holding register to streamline network communication.
The Python pymodbus library provides ModbusTcpClient to connect to servers and execute read or write function codes.
A Modbus server indicates an exception by adding 0x80 to the requested function code and returning an exception code.
Reading or writing an address outside the server's configured register range triggers exception code 02 for ILLEGAL DATA ADDRESS.
8-5: The industrial communication hierarchy connects real-time plant floor operational technology with enterprise information technology systems.
IO-Link enables bidirectional digital parameter setting and diagnostics with sensors across standard three-wire cables under IEC 61131-9.
OPC UA provides an object-oriented information model for machine data with binary transport over port 4840 and X.509v3 certificates.
The VDMA 40010 companion specification standardizes OPC UA information models for robotics across different manufacturers.
MQTT delivers lightweight publish-subscribe telemetry over TCP ports 1883 and 8883 using three defined Quality of Service levels.
8-6: The ISA/IEC 62443 standard establishes cybersecurity requirements for industrial automation based on shared responsibility across asset owners, integrators, and product suppliers.
Industrial demilitarized zones prevent direct corporate connections to control networks by requiring control zones to push data outward.
Configuring managed switch ports as static access ports and pruning default VLANs prevents unauthorized network trunk spoofing.
Time-Sensitive Networking standards provide deterministic connectivity and traffic scheduling over standard bridged Ethernet networks.
Wireshark analyzes captured Modbus TCP frames using the mbtcp display filter and Decode As overrides for non-standard network ports.
9-1: Reactive maintenance addresses equipment after failure, preventive maintenance follows scheduled operating intervals, and predictive maintenance initiates repairs from observed sensor data.
Maintenance logs recording faults and root causes must accompany sensor data to make equipment failure prediction effective.
Technicians wipe dust and oil off robot arms with approved cloths and solvents, never using damaging compressed air.
Cleaning dust inside the robot control box requires an electrostatic discharge vacuum cleaner to prevent damaging sensitive electronics.
Technicians must inspect robot arm and tool mounting bolts with a calibrated torque wrench after any heavy collision.
9-3: Technicians replace all joint flat rings together when one shows wear because the seals share the same operating environment.
Backdrive mode releases joint brakes so operators can manually move the arm to a safe position when close to a collision.
A properly engaged joint brake permits only one to two degrees of mechanical motion before hitting its brake pin.
Flexible couplings compensate for parallel shaft misalignment to prevent premature bearing failure on peripheral drive equipment.
Cable retraction systems and stress loops protect robot dress packs by maintaining bend radiuses and preventing pinch points.
9-4: Technicians ohm out multimeter test leads before testing to verify their resistance measurement is close to zero.
Continuity testing requires de-energizing circuits and isolating individual components from neighboring connections before taking measurements.
Fast-acting fuses operate too slowly to protect solid-state field sensors from short circuits or reverse polarity wiring mistakes.
Interposing relays provide galvanic isolation to eliminate electrical noise interference between the robot controller and external equipment.
In EtherCAT networks, dedicated Lost Link Counter registers track intermittent disconnects and an unexpected Working Counter invalidates frame data.
9-5: Updating revolution counters synchronizes robot axes by moving joints to their zero markings and saving the position in the service window.
Replacing a robot joint with a part from an incompatible model triggers error C364A1 indicating a robot type disagreement.
Dual Robot Calibration recalibrates kinematics across the full workspace so robots resume production after joint replacement without modifying waypoints.
Technicians must never remove controller SD cards or USB storage while power is on to avoid operating system and calibration corruption.
9-6: The Universal Robots Dashboard Server accepts human-readable text commands terminated by newlines over TCP port 29999.
Controlling a robot externally requires enabling Dashboard Server access and Remote Control mode in controller settings.
The robot mode RUNNING indicates that the arm has electrical power and released brakes, independent of program execution state.
The Dashboard Server recovery sequence sends close safety popup, unlock protective stop, and play to resume program execution.
Resuming a program after unlocking a protective stop restarts execution from where it stopped rather than from the beginning.
10-1: A factory acceptance test formally verifies that cell equipment meets engineering specifications and operates correctly before shipment to customer sites.
Mounting host directories into the URSim Docker container preserves exported robot programs and installation configurations across simulation restarts.
Programs must execute exact stops without blending wherever a robot gripper opens or closes during pick-and-place cycles.
A sequence chart maps numbered robotic actions to explicit starting conditions, forming the foundation of program logic and test sheets.
Simulated safety configurations demonstrate software limits but cannot replace physical risk assessments and validated safety hardware on real production cells.
10-2: The MoveIt Task Constructor decomposes complex pick-and-place tasks into transparent stage chains classified as generators, propagators, and connectors.
Wrapping candidate grasp pose generators in ComputeIK converts Cartesian target poses into valid joint configurations for the robot planner.
The PlanningSceneInterface applies collision objects like tables into the environment so motion planners automatically calculate collision-free trajectories around them.
ModifyPlanningScene stages attach the target object to the tool frame so MoveIt moves the object along with the arm during transport.
Mock hardware provides a lightweight environment for testing MoveIt planning pipelines without requiring physical robots or heavy physics simulation.
10-3: Connecting quadrature encoder channels to Arduino hardware interrupt pins enables reliable pulse counting without dropping edges during processor execution.
Calculating wheel rotational speed divides incremental encoder count changes by the output counts per revolution and elapsed sample time.
The TB6612FNG MOSFET driver exhibits smaller voltage drops than bipolar drivers like the L298N, delivering higher effective voltage to motors.
Velocity ramping increases speed setpoints gradually over time, reducing mechanical stress on gearboxes compared to abrupt step changes.
A supervisory state machine transitions into FAULT and cuts motor PWM whenever high commanded drive coincides with near-zero encoder feedback.
10-4: A cell monitor observes and reports equipment status without ever automatically acknowledging or resetting robot stops.
The monitor reads robot state from the Dashboard Server, handshake signals from Modbus registers and camera checks from ROS 2 topics.
Up to 16 on/off handshake signals can share one general-purpose Modbus register.
The monitor logs every state change with a time stamp and raises a warning, not a reset, when protective stops repeat.
Publishing an open-source ROS 2 package requires a descriptive README, an Apache 2.0 license, and contribution guidelines.
